sections.label: Digital government support disbursement
sections.summary: About 99% of Government transactions with citizens and businesses are completed digitally, enabling automatic support like U-Save rebates, CDC vouchers and Workfare top-ups.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: About 99% of Government transactions with citizens and businesses are now completed digitally from start to end, enabled by data.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Singaporean households automatically qualify for and receive support like U-Save rebates, our favourite Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers and Child LifeSG credits.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Lower-income workers automatically receive salary top-ups from the Workfare Income Supplement Scheme.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: And for our seniors, the Majulah package supports their healthcare and retirement, and the Senior Employment Credit supports their employment at the workplace.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: When support had to be rolled out quickly and at scale, for example through the Jobs Growth Incentive, the Government could calculate and disburse assistance more efficiently, without placing additional burden on Singaporeans and businesses during this difficult period.

sections.label: PSGA data sharing safeguards
sections.summary: Under the amended PSGA, public agencies may share data with trusted external partners only when three safeguards are met.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Under the amended PSGA, public agencies are allowed to share data with trusted external partners only when three safeguards are met.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: These are: (a) having a legitimate purpose for sharing; (b) the arrangement is specifically authorised by a Minister or the Minister's delegate; and (c) the external partner is bound by clear contractual terms of use, including data protection and security requirements.

sections.label: Criminal offences for external organisations
sections.summary: The Bill introduces criminal offences for individuals in external organisations, with help for smaller partners to meet requirements.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Where partners, especially smaller organisations, need to strengthen capabilities to meet these requirements, we will work with them so that safeguards are consistently applied.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: So, this Bill introduces criminal offences for individuals in external organisations.

sections.label: Equal penalties for external organisations
sections.summary: Individuals in external organisations face the same penalties public officers face for misusing shared data under the expanded PSGA offences.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: With these expanded PSGA offences, individuals in external organisations face the same level of penalties that public officers are currently subject to for misusing shared data.

sections.label: MOE data use check
sections.summary: As the PSGA was not explicit that MOE's data could be used for other purposes, MOE spent an extra month checking the threshold.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: As the PSGA was not explicit that the data MOE had could be used for other purposes, MOE spent an extra month checking if this new use met the threshold for public interest or consent exclusions.

sections.label: Health Information Bill framework
sections.summary: The Government will introduce a Health Information Bill setting out a framework for the National Electronic Health Record, complementary to the PSGA.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: The Government will also be introducing a Health Information Bill (HIB), which will set out a framework governing information contributed to and accessed from the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR).

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Both the PSGA and the HIB are complementary Bills.

sections.label: Cybersecurity safeguards for external partners
sections.summary: External partners must meet cybersecurity and data security safeguards through Terms of Use, with one exception for MHA.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Cybersecurity and data security safeguards matching those under the HIB will be required through the Terms of Use for external partners.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: There is one exception relating to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

sections.label: MHA consent and data assessments
sections.summary: MHA will seek consent and conduct personal data protection impact assessments, which cannot be waived without consulting MOH.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: MHA will seek consent from personnel and conduct personal data protection impact assessments.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
sentences.text: Both requirements cannot be waived without consulting the Ministry of Health (MOH) first.

sections.label: Data sharing benefits for residents
sections.summary: Information sharing supports GST Vouchers, Workfare Income Supplement, and business schemes for vulnerable workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: They are lived realities for our residents and businesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: We see this in the seamless sharing of information at the backend: whether in the delivery of the Goods and Services Tax Vouchers (GSTV) and Workfare Income Supplement, or in businesses applying for schemes such as the Enabling Employment Credit and Senior Employment Credit to support vulnerable workers, and many more examples shared by Minister of State earlier.

sections.label: Extending PSGA benefits externally
sections.summary: The Bill seeks to extend PSGA benefits by enabling trusted data sharing with external partners.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Singaporeans recognise the significant benefits that the PSGA has delivered within Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: This Bill seeks to extend those benefits by enabling trusted data sharing with external partners.

sections.label: Thresholds and healthcare data scope
sections.summary: Questions cover what thresholds, principles and public-interest considerations apply, and the scope of healthcare data sharing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: What thresholds, what principles and public-interest considerations must be met before data move beyond the public sector?

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Second, the scope of data sharing, particularly in relation to healthcare data.

sections.label: Appointing and assessing external partners
sections.summary: Once data-sharing is deemed appropriate, the question is how external partners are appointed and assessed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Third, once data-sharing is deemed appropriate, how do we appoint and assess external partners?

sections.label: Extending data sharing to external partners
sections.summary: The Bill extends Public Sector (Governance) Act benefits by sharing data with external partners while protecting Singaporeans' data and requiring high standards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: (In Malay):   There have been many benefits brought by the Public Sector (Governance) Act in strengthening the Government's service delivery.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: This Bill seeks to extend those benefits through data sharing with external partners, namely organisations outside the public sector.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: In this endeavour, it is important for us to enhance our capability to share data securely, protect the data of Singaporeans and ensure that the selected external partners comply with the same high standards that citizens expect from the Government.

sections.label: Standards required of external partners
sections.summary: The passage asks what equivalent standards will be required of external partners as data sharing is extended to them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: As we extend data sharing to external partners, what equivalent standards will be required of them?

sections.label: Differentiated standards by data sensitivity
sections.summary: The passage asks whether differentiated standards can apply based on the classification and sensitivity of data shared.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Can there be differentiated standards based on the classification and sensitivity of data shared?

sections.label: Support, retention and accountability for partners
sections.summary: The passage seeks clarification on funding support, data retention, secure deletion, audit trails and how equivalence, compliance and accountability are assured.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Some social service organisations, for example, are exceptionally effective at engaging vulnerable seniors or families in need; yet, may not have the resource or technical capability to immediately meet stringent digital standards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: In this regard, I seek clarification on whether the Government would consider providing support through targeted funding or capability-building programmes to help such partners strengthen their digital resilience.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: As we approach the Budget period, this may be a timely area for consideration, ensuring that trust and inclusion advance together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: I seek clarification on how long external partners may retain this data shared, how proper care, retention and eventual secure deletion of data would be enforced, whether responsibility for ensuring data wiping rests with the individual Ministries or centrally and whether Ministries are adequately resourced to manage these audit trails over time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: The question before us is how equivalence is assured, how compliance is enforced and how accountability is maintained when trust is delegated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: These clarifications are intended to ensure that we scale data sharing not just efficiently, but responsibly – delivering the best public good while safeguarding the data, privacy and trust of Singaporeans.

sections.label: Expanded data sharing through Ministerial directions
sections.summary: The Bill expands data sharing to authorise data use, sharing with non-public sector persons and re-identification of anonymised information through Ministerial directions.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Bill before us today moves us from a framework that, on the whole, allowed data to be shared between public agencies and subject to rules and regulations about such sharing and use, to one which expands the sharing of data expressly authorising: one, the use of data; two, the sharing of data with non-public sector persons; and three, even the re-identification of previously anonymised information – all through Ministerial directions and further authorisations, that is, data sharing and use directions given by a Minister.

sections.label: Agencies' difficulties in last five years
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister to clarify how many times in the last five years agencies ran into difficulties providing necessary services.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In this regard, I understand that there will be grounds and limited instances in which data will be shared.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, for a full understanding of the difficulties faced, could the Minister clarify, in the last five years, how many times have agencies run into difficulties in providing necessary services to the community?

sections.label: Data sharing and use directions
sections.summary: The Bill's amendments let Ministers issue data sharing and use directions and authorise sharing data with non-public sector persons.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Under the proposed amendments to this Bill, Ministers will be able to issue data sharing and use directions, and be allowed to further authorise sharing of data with non-public sector persons.

sections.label: Oversight of directions
sections.summary: The question asks what oversight mechanisms ensure a direction is not overly broad or made erroneously.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Could the Minister thus clarify, what would be the oversight mechanisms to be applied in ensuring that a direction is not overly broad nor made erroneously?

sections.label: Commercially sensitive data consideration
sections.summary: The question asks whether and how data sharing and use directions will explicitly require consideration of commercially sensitive data.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Could the Minister thus clarify about whether and how the proposed data sharing and use directions will explicitly require consideration and evaluation of data that could be commercially sensitive?

sections.label: Assessment factors for authorisation
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Minister must assess listed factors and whether they are documented in writing for each authorisation.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For instance, must the Minister assess the sensitivity classification of the data, the proportionality between privacy, intrusion and public benefit, whether less intrusive alternatives exist and the data recipients' security posture, and are these factors documented in writing for each authorisation?

sections.label: Re-identification, concerns, breaches, redress
sections.summary: The question asks what instances lead to re-identification, avenues to raise concerns, how breaches are communicated, and how individuals seek redress.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Can the Minister thus clarify: one, what instances would lead to re-identification; two, what avenues exists to raise concerns; three, how will breaches by non-public sector persons be communicated, particularly to affected citizens; and four, how can individuals seek redress in this system that has an increasing number of third-party partners or contractors?

sections.label: Strengthening governance of expanded powers
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to consider how Parliament is updated, how Singaporeans get recourse, and how sensitive information is safeguarded.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, I hope that as we expand the executive's discretion about the use of our data out of necessity, we strengthen rather than dilute the governance framework around these increased powers.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Thus, could the Minister consider, first, how Parliament can be kept updated and meaningfully informed about the use of these powers.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Second, how Singaporeans can have clearer avenues for recourse.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And finally, how can commercial and personal sensitive information be more explicitly safeguarded, even if the use and sharing of such data is subject to Ministerial discretion.

sections.label: Data sharing public interest purposes
sections.summary: The amendment Bill requires any data sharing with external partners to remain tied to the seven public interest purposes in the PSGA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Under the amendment Bill, any sharing of data with external partners must still be tied to the same seven public interest purposes set out in PSGA.

sections.label: Ministerial direction for external sharing
sections.summary: The amendment Bill requires any sharing with external partners to be backed by a Ministerial direction.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Under the amendment Bill, any sharing with external partners must be backed by a Ministerial direction.

sections.label: Criminal penalties for external partners
sections.summary: The amendment Bill holds external partners receiving public sector data to the same criminal penalties as public officers for misuse, with fines up to $5,000, imprisonment up to two years, or both.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The amendment Bill addresses the gap without adding unnecessary compliance burdens for partners, requiring external partners who receive public sector data to be held to the same criminal penalties as public officers if they misuse it, whether through unauthorised disclosure, improper use or re-identifying anonymised information without approval.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: These offences carry the same penalties already set out in the PSGA, which are fines of up to $5,000, imprisonment of up to two years, or both.

sections.label: Question on regular audits
sections.summary: A Member asks whether agencies must conduct regular audits to confirm Ministerial direction obligations are met throughout the partnership.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: I am glad to hear the Minister of State say in her speech that before sharing data, agencies are responsible for assessing whether each partner has the systems, processes and competencies to handle Government data securely.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: I would suggest and would like to ask if the agencies are also required to conduct regular audits to confirm that the obligations in the Ministerial directions are being met in practice throughout the partnership.

sections.label: Risk-based data security approach
sections.summary: The Member suggests agencies adopt a risk-based approach, with deeper technical assessments for higher-risk data flows and lighter treatment for lower-risk projects, recognising independent certifications or existing audits.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: What I am suggesting is not imposing additional burdens.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: But I suggest that perhaps we consider not imposing a one‑size‑fits‑all data security burden – I believe the Minister of State did touch on this point – but perhaps that agencies could adopt a risk‑based approach that looks at higher‑risk data flows, undergoing deeper technical assessments, and at lower‑risk or time‑limited projects with a lighter touch.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Where appropriate, agencies can also recognise independent certifications or existing audits rather than duplicating effort.

sections.label: PSGA intent on secure data use
sections.summary: The intent of the PSGA is not to prevent the use of data but how to use it securely.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: At the end of the day, the intent of the PSGA is not to prevent the use of data but how to use it securely.

sections.label: Data breach damage and trust
sections.summary: The passage states that once a data breach happens the damage is done, and the Bill centres on honouring trust when Singaporeans share information.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Because once a data breach happens, the damage is already done.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: We must remember that at the heart of the Bill is a simple promise – that when Singaporeans share their information, that their trust will be honoured.

sections.label: PSGA safeguards and TraceTogether access
sections.summary: The passage says proactive safeguards make PSGA safeguards real, and notes Singaporeans learned in January 2021 that Police had access to TraceTogether data under the Criminal Procedure Code.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: When agencies and external organisations take that proactive approach and put the safeguards in place, the safeguards in the PSGA then become safeguards in practice rather than just on paper, serving Singaporeans effectively and giving Singaporeans confidence that their information is protected every day.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In January 2021, Singaporeans learned that Police had access to TraceTogether data under the Criminal Procedure Code.

sections.label: Expedited COVID-19 Amendment Bill passage
sections.summary: The backlash led to expedited passage in February 2021 of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment) Bill restricting access to seven serious offence categories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The backlash led to the expedited passage in February 2021 of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment) Bill restricting access to seven serious offence categories.

sections.label: Data flow and re-identification power
sections.summary: The passage states data can now flow to private companies, contractors and vendors, and introduces a power to re-identify anonymised information.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Data can now flow to private companies, contractors and vendors, and introduces a power to re-identify anonymised information.

sections.label: Citizens' data sharing rights
sections.summary: The passage states citizens have no right to know when data is shared with a private company, no mechanism to find which companies hold it, and no way to ensure benefit from its value.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under this Bill, a citizen has no right to know when their data is shared with a private company, no mechanism to find out which companies hold their data and no way to ensure they benefit from the value that data creates.

sections.label: Proposed formal public review
sections.summary: The passage asks whether committing to a review now is better than legislating later, and whether the Minister would commit to a formal public review within five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Would it not be better to commit to a review now, than to legislate in the possible crisis of confidence later?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, question three: would the Minister commit to a formal public review within five years, including the directions issued, the data shared and whether the safeguards have been adequate?

sections.label: Data sharing transparency commitments
sections.summary: Speaker says data sharing needs transparency, citing TraceTogether, and asks for a public register, benefit tracking, five-year review and accountability fixes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Data will flow to where it creates value.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But we should learn the lessons of TraceTogether.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: TraceTogether taught us that non-transparency about data sharing has costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Transparency is what makes data sharing sustainable in the long term.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, we will continue to ask for three commitments: a public register, a mechanism to track and report citizen benefit, and a formal review within five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And I have flagged two gaps in organisational accountability that should be addressed.

sections.label: Safeguards for external data sharing
sections.summary: The Bill provides three safeguards for data sharing with external partners: Ministerial authorisation, terms of use with data protection requirements, and criminal penalties for misuse.

sentences.speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Bill provides three layers of safeguards for data sharing with external partners – Ministerial authorisation, terms of use which impose data protection requirements and criminal penalties for misuse.

sections.label: Health information requests safeguards
sections.summary: Speaker notes consent and impact assessment requirements for public sector health information requests, HIB's NEHR prohibition, and urges rarer requests, scrutiny, review and annual reports.

sentences.speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: A particularly sensitive area involves requests for health information by public sector agencies for employment or insurance purposes.

sentences.speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: It is comforting to know that when public sector agencies request health information from MOH for employment or insurance purposes under PSGA, they must first seek consent from individuals and conduct a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment.

sentences.speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The HIB prohibits NEHR access for employment or insurance purposes to prevent discrimination.

sentences.speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I note that the Bill requires individual consent and a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment for such requests, with MOH oversight.

sentences.speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: But I urge the Government to go further – commit that such requests will be rare and exceptional, subject them to close scrutiny and independent review, and publish annual reports detailing the number and nature of such requests to ensure transparency and accountability.

sections.label: Examples of improved outcomes
sections.summary: Speaker asks the Minister of State to share concrete examples across Government of how the Bill will improve outcomes for Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: First, can the Minister of State share a range of concrete examples across the Government of how this Bill will improve outcomes for Singaporeans beyond what she has shared earlier?

sections.label: Principles for sharing data
sections.summary: Speaker asks what key principles decide what to share, with whom and how much, and how purpose limitation and data minimisation will be ensured.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: What are the key principles for deciding what to share, with whom and how much?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: How will the Government ensure purpose limitation and data minimisation is done, so that we share what is needed and not more than what is needed, and not longer than what is needed?

sections.label: Cybersecurity expectations across partners
sections.summary: Speaker asks the Minister of State for the Government's approach to setting cybersecurity expectations that are robust, clear and workable across different partners.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: With that in mind, I would like to ask the Minister of State the Government’s approach to setting cybersecurity expectations that are robust but also clear and workable across different partners?

sections.label: Public Service Governance Bill data sharing
sections.summary: The Public Service (Governance) Bill lets public agencies share and use data across agencies and with non-public sector partners.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: As Minister of State Jasmin Lau shared, I note that in tandem with the HIB, the Public Service (Governance) Bill complements and allows the Government to deliver better social services to Singaporeans nationwide, by permitting public agencies to share and use data across agencies, as well as with non-public sector partners.

sections.label: Safeguards for shared data
sections.summary: The Member asks the Minister what safeguards will protect data shared with non-public sector organisations from cyberattacks and breaches.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: First, I would like to ask the Minister to clarify what safeguards will be put in place to ensure that data shared with non-public sector organisations is safe from malicious third-party cyberattacks and data breaches.

sections.label: External partners maintaining safeguards
sections.summary: The Member asks how external partners will be expected to keep up and maintain safeguards before receiving shared data from public agencies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: As hackers use sophisticated techniques to evade detection, they lurk in networks to spy over the long term, to steal sensitive information or disrupt essential services, among other objectives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Therefore, my question is, how will external partners be expected to keep up and maintain safeguards, before they can receive shared data from public agencies?

sections.label: Offence for improper data disclosure
sections.summary: The amendment states it is an offence for employees or officers of non-public sector organisations to improperly disclose or use data.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The amendment currently states that it is an offence for organisations to carry out improper disclosure or use of data/information by individual employees or officers of non-public sector organisations.

sections.label: Ministerial authorisation for sharing information
sections.summary: Under amended sections 4(5) to 4(8), a public agency may share information with non-public sector persons only with further Ministerial authorisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Under the amended sections 4(5) to 4(8), a public agency may share information with non-public sector persons only with further authorisation from the Minister.

sections.label: Auditable register and penalties
sections.summary: The Member asks about an auditable register of authorisations and whether penalties of up to $5,000 or two years' imprisonment deter negligence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Third, could the Government consider maintaining an auditable register of future authorisations, with anonymised statistics published annually?

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Bill introduces offences for unauthorised disclosure of non-personal data by employees of external partners, with penalties of up to $5,000 or two years' imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Where large datasets are mishandled, will these penalties sufficiently deter negligence?

sections.label: External partners data standards
sections.summary: PAP MPs stressed external partners must meet the same high standards as the Government, with public interest tests, oversight and accountability, and alignment with the upcoming HIB.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Many PAP MPs today have rightly stressed that when data leaves the public sector, external partners must meet the same high standards as the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: With clear public interest tests, stronger oversight and firm accountability, including how this Bill aligns with the HIB that is upcoming.

sections.label: Commitment on data use
sections.summary: The commitment is to use data to protect, not stigmatise, and to share data to connect, not surveil.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: So, let us be clear about our commitment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: We will use data to protect, not to stigmatise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: We will share data to connect, not to surveil.

sections.label: Clear public service objective
sections.summary: Data will only be shared when there is a clear public service objective.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: Likewise, data will only be shared when there is a clear public service objective.

sections.label: Further authorisation second layer
sections.summary: The Bill adds a second layer of checks called the further authorisation for cases of sharing with external partners.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: What we are adding is a second layer of checks referred to as the "further authorisation" in the Bill for cases of sharing with external partners.

sections.label: Authorisation states purpose and parties
sections.summary: Each authorisation must clearly state the purpose for sharing, the scope of data to be shared, and the specific external parties receiving the data.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: Each authorisation must clearly state the purpose for sharing the scope of data to be shared and the specific external parties receiving the data.

sections.label: Assessing external partner safeguards
sections.summary: Public agencies must assess the external partner's ability to meet the Terms of Use and impose them, including data security and protection safeguards.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: Even if there is a valid purpose and proper authorisation, public agencies must assess the external partner's ability to meet the requirements in the Terms of Use and impose these terms on them.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: These Terms of Use will include data security and protection safeguards, such as using anti-malware software with up-to-date signatures and performing regular vulnerability assessments.

sections.label: Anonymised data for external partners
sections.summary: Where identifiable personal data is not needed, anonymised data will be provided to external partners instead.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: The starting point is this: where identifiable personal data is not needed, anonymised data will be provided to external partners instead.

sections.label: Health information employment insurance rules
sections.summary: Health information used for employment and insurance purposes has additional Public Service requirements to seek consent and conduct a data protection impact assessment under the PSGA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: In the instance of health information, which Dr Choo had asked about, for health information that is used for employment and insurance purposes in particular, there will be additional requirements under the Public Service's rules to seek consent and to conduct a personal data protection impact assessment under the PSGA.

sections.label: Re-identification for public sector objectives
sections.summary: Re-identification of anonymised data can be allowed only when it meets public sector objectives.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: Re-identification of anonymised data can be allowed only when it meets public sector objectives.

sections.label: Tiering cybersecurity requirements not advisable
sections.summary: Tiering cybersecurity requirements so that smaller entities face less stringent standards is not advisable, though well-intentioned.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: While well-intentioned, tiering cybersecurity requirements so that smaller entities face less stringent standards is not advisable.

sections.label: Bill amends PDPA offences
sections.summary: The Bill amends the PDPA so offences relating to personal data still apply, covering all Government-shared data under PDPA or PSGA penalties.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: The Bill amends the PDPA to make clear that offences relating to personal data under the PDPA will still apply so that individuals that intentionally carry out unauthorised actions can be taken to task.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: And this means that all data shared by Government, be it personal or non-personal data, is covered either by PDPA or PSGA in terms of penalties for misuse.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: The penalties are aligned with current PDPA offences for external partners and PSGA offences for public officials.

sections.label: Significant data incident notification requirements
sections.summary: Public agencies must be accountable for significant data incidents, and affected individuals will be notified unless it would adversely impact public interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: When significant data incidents occur, we have strict requirements for public agencies to be accountable to the public and to affected individuals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: And when incidents are likely to result in significant harm or impact on individuals or entities, affected individuals will be notified, except where it would adversely impact public interest.

sections.label: TraceTogether data use restricted
sections.summary: Parliament passed a Bill amending the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act to restrict TraceTogether data use to serious offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: Parliament subsequently passed the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment) Bill to restrict the use of TraceTogether data to serious offences.

sections.label: Clarifying non-personal data liability
sections.summary: A member asks whether organisational statutory liability exists for non-personal data and requests a public register of Ministerial directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
sentences.text: I just want to clarify, because I think she may have misunderstood what was my fifth question.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
sentences.text: I was saying that there is no organisational statutory liability for those handling non-personal data, and I think she made some references to contractual obligations as well as something about personal — so, I just want to clarify that it is organisational statutory liability for non-personal data, does it exist or not?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
sentences.text: Another thing I would like to bring up, which I do not think she has answered, is my request for a public register of all these Ministerial directions.

sections.label: Organisations liable for data misuse
sections.summary: A member says organisations are liable for data misuse under the existing PDPA and Terms of Use, citing Australia as an example.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
sentences.text: Australia does it, and I think it is quite a sound legislative principle. so, these are my supplementary questions for now.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: I spent quite a bit of time just now explaining how organisations will be liable if they misuse data: there is an existing PDPA, as well as Terms of Use.

sections.label: Public register considered later
sections.summary: A speaker says the public register will be considered as feasible as more experience with the Bill is gained.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
sentences.text: On the point about public register, I think I mentioned in my speech, that we will consider what is possible, what is feasible, as we get more experience with the Bill.
